title: Paul Boasts About His Weakness
overview: Paul pushes back against rival teachers in Corinth by reluctantly boasting, listing not his successes but his sufferings and weaknesses.

parts.label: A protective, jealous love (vv. 1-4)
parts.note: Paul asks the church to bear with a little foolishness, meaning talk about himself, because he pictures them as a bride he has promised to Christ and fears she will be led astray. Just as the serpent fooled Eve, newcomers are preaching another Jesus and a different message, and the Corinthians are accepting it far too easily.

parts.label: Why he worked for free (vv. 5-11)
parts.note: The top apostles Paul says he is not behind are most likely the visiting rivals rather than Peter and the other original apostles, though scholars debate this. Teachers were usually paid by patrons, so his refusal of Corinthian money, while accepting gifts from churches in Macedonia, may have looked odd or even insulting; he insists he did it out of love, not to keep them at a distance.

parts.label: Fakes in disguise (vv. 12-15)
parts.note: Paul keeps refusing payment so his rivals cannot claim to be his equals or accuse him of preaching for profit. He calls them false apostles disguised as servants of what is right, just as Satan can pose as an angel of light, and says their end will match what they have done.

parts.label: Playing the fool (vv. 16-21a)
parts.note: Paul admits that bragging is not how the Lord would speak, but since his rivals boast, he will play along as a fool. His tone is sharply ironic: the Corinthians, so wise, put up with leaders who control, exploit and even strike them, and he says with mock shame that he was too weak to treat them that way.

parts.label: A record of suffering (vv. 21b-29)
parts.note: Paul matches his rivals' Jewish heritage, then lists hardships instead of achievements: 39 lashes five times (synagogue discipline that stopped one short of the limit of 40 in the Jewish law), beatings with rods, a stoning, shipwrecks, hunger and constant danger. On top of all this, he carries daily worry for every church and feels each person's struggles as his own.

parts.label: Escape in a basket (vv. 30-33)
parts.note: If he must boast, Paul will boast about weakness, and he ends with an undignified story of being lowered from the wall of Damascus in a basket to escape a governor under King Aretas. Some scholars suggest this pokes fun at the Roman honor given to the first soldier up an enemy wall, since Paul's chosen memory is going down one.

disagreement: Scholars and Christians differ on who exactly Paul's rivals were, whether Jewish Christian missionaries tied to Jerusalem or teachers prizing polished speech and impressive displays, and this shapes what the chapter is warning against.
think: When you decide whether to trust someone, what tells you more about them: their strengths and successes, or how they handle their weaknesses and setbacks?
